Q: Printing current time in milliseconds or nanoseconds with printf builtin A:

bash v5 and $EPOCHREALTIME

  • EPOCHREALTIME floating point value with micro-second granularity
  • EPOCHSECONDS the number of seconds since the Unix Epoch

Correct way

Simply:

IFS=. read ESEC NSEC <<<$EPOCHREALTIME
printf '%(%F:%T)T.%06.0f\n' $ESEC $NSEC
2024-05-19:11:31:09.582696

printf '%(%a %b %d %T)T.%06.0f %(%Y)T\n' $ESEC $NSEC $ESEC
Sun May 19 11:31:09.582696 2024

Or if you really don't need to store values as variables:

printf '%(%F %T)T.%06.0f\n' ${EPOCHREALTIME/./ }
2024-05-19 11:10:47.434792

or

printf '%(%a %b %d %Y %T)T.%06.0f\n' ${EPOCHREALTIME/./ }
Sun May 19 2024 11:12:13.539451

But take care to not use $EPOCHREALTIME twice consecutively!!

printf '%(%a %b %d %T)T.%06.0f %(%Y)T\n' ${EPOCHREALTIME/./ } ${EPOCHREALTIME%.*}
Sun May 19 11:26:18.666577 2024

It may seem correct, but this is subject to an issue! See further.

I often use in my scripts,

something like:

logLine() {
    local ms;
    printf -v ms %.3f $EPOCHREALTIME;
    printf '%(%F %T)T.%s %s\n' ${ms%.*} ${ms#*.} "$*"
}

in order to round value to milliseconds.

1. About $EPOCHREALTIME

Please note:

EPOCHREALTIME
  Each time this parameter is referenced, it expands to the number
  of seconds since the Unix Epoch (see time(3)) as a floating
  point value with micro-second granularity.

So, if I ask for same variable twice in the same line:

echo $EPOCHREALTIME...  $EPOCHREALTIME 
1572000683.886830... 1572000683.886840

or more clearly:

printf "%s\n" ${EPOCHREALTIME#*.} ${EPOCHREALTIME#*.}
761893
761925

echo $(( -10#${EPOCHREALTIME#*.} + 10#${EPOCHREALTIME#*.} ))
37

So querying this twice for building the integer part and fractional part could lead to issues: On the same line, the first access to $EPOCHREALTIME could give: NNN1.999995, then next: NNN2.000002. Then the result will become: NNN1.000002 with 1000000 micro-second error.

2. WARNING! About mixing $EPOCHSECONDS and $EPOCHREALTIME

Using both together not only leads to the first mentioned bug!

$EPOCHSECONDS uses system call to time() which is not updated constantly, while $EPOCHREALTIME uses system call to gettimeofday()! So results could differ a lot:

I found This answer to time() and gettimeofday() return different seconds with good explanation.

Trying to zoom on differences between $EPOCHSECONDS and $EPOCHREALTIME, on my host:

epochVariableDiff () {
    local errcnt=0 lasterrcnt v1 v2 v3 us vals line
    printf  '%3s %13s - %13s - %13s . %9s\n' \
        cnt 'printf %()T' EPOCHSECONDS EPOCHREALTIME MuSecs
    while ((errcnt==0)) || ((errcnt>lasterrcnt)); do
        lasterrcnt=$errcnt
        printf -v vals '%(%s)T %s %s' -1 $EPOCHSECONDS $EPOCHREALTIME
        IFS=$' .' read v1 v2 v3 us <<<"$vals"
        [ "$v1" = "$v2" ] && [ "$v2" = "$v3" ] || ((errcnt++))
        [ $errcnt -eq 1 ] && echo "$line"
        printf -v line '%3d %13s - %13s - %13s . %9s' $errcnt $v1 $v2 $v3 $us
        printf "%s\r" "$line"
        ((errcnt)) && echo "$line"
        read -t ${1:-.0002}
    done
}
  • Nota: I use read -t instead of sleep, because sleep is not builtin
  • Nota 2: You could play with argument of function to change value of read timeout (sleep)

This could render something like:

$ epochVariableDiff .0002
cnt   printf %()T -  EPOCHSECONDS - EPOCHREALTIME .    MuSecs
  0    1730877514 -    1730877514 -    1730877514 .    999618
  1    1730877514 -    1730877514 -    1730877515 .    000110
  2    1730877514 -    1730877514 -    1730877515 .    000965
  3    1730877514 -    1730877514 -    1730877515 .    001500
  4    1730877514 -    1730877514 -    1730877515 .    001996
  5    1730877514 -    1730877514 -    1730877515 .    002591
  6    1730877514 -    1730877514 -    1730877515 .    003124
  7    1730877514 -    1730877514 -    1730877515 .    003627
  8    1730877514 -    1730877514 -    1730877515 .    004106
  9    1730877514 -    1730877514 -    1730877515 .    004595
 10    1730877514 -    1730877514 -    1730877515 .    005090
 11    1730877514 -    1730877514 -    1730877515 .    005564
 11    1730877515 -    1730877515 -    1730877515 .    006010

Where:

  • As explained in introduction, expanding $EPOCH* twice consecutively could lead to almost 1'000'000 microseconds error, as is shown at output line 0 (with 999'618 µs).
  • After 11 loop, with .2 ms delay, $EPOCHSECONDS shows 1730877514 (.00) when $EPOCHREALTIME show 1730877515.0056!
  • Integer part of $EPOCHREALTIME could increase more than 5'564 microseconds before $EPOCHSECONDS (on my host, line 11)!

Nota: This seems to be linked to some bug, result could differ a lot between different hosts or on same host after reboot, and other things... Strangely I could reproduce them on a lot of different hosts (Intel Core, Intel Xeon, Amd64..) but not on raspberry pi!? (Same Debian bash v5.0.3(1)-release), different kernel version.

Correct: This is not a bug! Mixing time() and gettimeofday() is a bug!

So avoid using both together!!!

3. About printf "..%06.0f"

Nota: I use %06.0f instead of %d to ensure that $NSEC is interpreted as a decimal (float) (preventing octal interpretation if variable begin by 0).

Compare:

printf "nn.%06.0f\n" 012345
nn.012345

printf "nn.%06.0f\n" 098765
nn.098765

and

printf "nn.%d\n" 012345
nn.5349

printf "nn.%d\n" 098765
-bash: printf: 098765: invalid octal number
nn.0

Sample run: Showing time at beginning of each seconds...

Little test:

wait until next second, then print current time with micro-seconds

while ! read -sn 1 -t .$(( 1000000 - 10#${EPOCHREALTIME#*.} )) _; do
    IFS=. read ESEC NSEC <<< $EPOCHREALTIME
    printf '%(%F:%T)T.%06.0f\n' $ESEC $NSEC
done

You could end this test by pressing any key.

2023-01-06:17:28:51.000135
2023-01-06:17:28:52.000095
2023-01-06:17:28:53.000109
2023-01-06:17:28:54.000108
2023-01-06:17:28:55.000132
2023-01-06:17:28:56.000166
2023-01-06:17:28:57.000099

More flexible:

delay=5.5
printf -v delay '%.6f' $delay
delay=${delay/.}
while toSlp=00000$(( delay - ${EPOCHREALTIME/.}%delay))
        printf -v toSlp %.4f ${toSlp::-6}.${toSlp: -6}
        ! read -sn 1 -t $toSlp _
  do
    IFS=. read ESEC NSEC <<< $EPOCHREALTIME
    printf '%(%F:%T)T.%06.0f\n' $ESEC $NSEC
done
2024-05-19:12:08:14.502578
2024-05-19:12:08:20.002743
2024-05-19:12:08:25.505742

Q: NodeJS Docker container build failing - npm ERR! code EAccess A:

This is most likely a file ownership issue rather than an Alpine change. By default, Docker copies files into the image as root, even if you've switched to a non-root user. Since npm install may need to read or update package-lock.json and create node_modules, it fails with EACCES when the app user doesn't own those files.

A clean fix is to copy the files with the correct ownership:

COPY --chown=app:app package*.json ./
...
COPY --chown=app:app . .

This makes the copied files belong to the same user that runs the application, avoiding the permission error without falling back to running the container as root.

Q: Detecting if a key is HELD down - python A:

You can use set to detect if a key is pressed to process your code and reset when the key is released.

To give you a better understanding of pynput here is a tidbit from their documentation.
Under the subsection of pynput Package Documentation -> Monitoring the keyboard

Synchronous event listening for the keyboard listener
To simplify scripting, synchronous event listening is supported through the utility class pynput.keyboard.Events. This class supports reading single events in a non-blocking fashion, as well as iterating over all events.

Copied from PyCharm's Documentation Popup Box.

pynput.keyboard.Events
A keyboard event listener supporting synchronous iteration over the events.
Possible events are:
:class: Events.Press A key was pressed.
:class: Events.Release A key was released.

pynput.keyboard.Events will block the main thread until a key is pressed and will continue blocking when the key is released.

from pynput.keyboard import Events, Key, KeyCode

hotkey_sets = [
    {Key.ctrl_l, Key.alt_l, 65},  # LEFT CTRL + LEFT ALT + A
    {Key.esc}
]

pressed = set()

with Events() as events:
    for event in events:
        if type(event.key) is Key:
            key = event.key
            print(type(event.key).__name__, type(event).__name__, event.key.name, event.key.value.char, event.key.value.vk, sep = ', ')
        if type(event.key) is KeyCode:
            key = event.key.vk
            print(type(event.key).__name__, type(event).__name__, event.key.char, event.key.vk, sep = ', ')

        if type(event) is Events.Press:
            if key not in pressed:
                pressed.add(key)
                if key == Key.f8:
                    # Execute Your Code
                    continue

                # To further explain how you can use set to detect if a key is pressed, I've added this.
                # for hotkeys in hotkey_sets:
                #     if all([_key in pressed for _key in hotkeys]):
                #         for _key in hotkeys:
                #             if _key == key:
                #                 if hotkeys == hotkey_sets[0]:
                #                     print('LEFT CTRL + LEFT ALT + A')  # Execute Your Code
                #                     break
                #                     
                #                 elif hotkeys == hotkey_sets[1]:
                #                     print('ESC')  # Execute Your Code
                #                     break
                # 
                #         else:
                #             continue
                # 
                #         break

        elif type(event) is Events.Release:
            if key in pressed:
                pressed.remove(key)
                if key == Key.f8:
                    # Reset After Release
                    pass
                elif key == Key.esc:
                    break

Q: Exclude variable-length suffix from python list/array which could be zero A:

As far as I know, there is no built-in way of doing this but you could write a function:

def get_last_n(full_list, n):
    return full_list if n==0 else full_list[:-n]

and then use it in your code like this:

shortened_list = get_last_n(full_list, n)

This isn't that much shorter but at least it lowers the chance of a typo.

Edit: Or, another probably better solution (though a little bit hacky/code-golf-y):

shortened_list = full_list[:-n or 1<<99]

The way this works is:

  • If n>0, -n is truthy so is the index used (the desired outcome)
  • If n==0, -n is 0 is falsey so the or operator takes the second argument (which is 299) so this takes the first 299 items of the list, which is the whole list (any list larger than that has no chance of ever fitting into memory)

The advantage of this is that it should now be compatible with numpy/etc. (though I haven't tested it). For example,

shortened_array = full_array[:,:,:-n]
# Written as
shortened_array = full_array[:,:,:-n or 1<<99]

Q: Migration HSQLDB to MySQL using MySQL Workbench 6.2 A:

I just used RazorSQL successfully to migrate from a HSQLDB (split from LibreOffice Base) to MySQL. When connected to your HSQLDB, use Menu -> DB Tools -> Database Conversion. The created SQL file can then be imported with MySQL Workbench

To migrate the views use Menu -> DB Tools -> Generate DDL and leave only Generate View DDL ticked. The resulting SQL can then be executed in MySQL Workbench.

Q: Expr. does not compile but decltype(expr.) does A:

You cannot pass a NoMove object to variadic parameters .... Passing it requires NoMove be copyable/movable which it is not.

From variadic_arguments, emphasis mine:

Non-POD class types(until C++11)Scoped enumerations and class types with an eligible non-trivial copy constructor, an eligible non-trivial move constructor, or a non-trivial destructor(since C++11) are conditionally-supported in potentially-evaluated calls with implementation-defined semantics (these types are always supported in unevaluated calls).

So with regular calls, the behavior is up-to the compiler; Does it support it? Does it copy/move it, take by reference? ...

With unevaluated context (as decltype), those type are always supported (probably for SFINAE support).
